hints: Think about what gas a leaf must take in during the day for photosynthesis, and which pore it must open to get it.
Remember that the inside of the leaf is wet, so what else can move through that same open pore but in the opposite direction?
Link the outward movement to a gradient - from high to low water potential between the leaf air spaces and the outside air.
walkthrough:
Why Leaves Must Open Up**
Leaves need carbon dioxide for photosynthesis in the light. The only way in is by diffusion through open stomata in the epidermis. You cannot have photosynthesis without gas exchange.

Why Water Must Leave**
The mesophyll cell walls and air spaces inside the leaf are moist, so the air inside has a high water potential. Outside air is usually drier with lower water potential. When stomata are open, water vapour inevitably evaporates and then diffuses out down this water potential gradient. That loss is transpiration.

Final answer: Stomata open to allow diffusion in of carbon dioxide required for photosynthesis. Water vapour in the moist air spaces diffuses out through the open stomata down the water potential gradient to the outside air.

hints: Start from the water molecule itself - it is polar, so what type of bond forms between one water molecule and the next?
Now think of two different attractions: water to water versus water to the xylem wall - what are their names?
Consider what happens when water is pulled up from the top - how do these attractions stop the column snapping?
walkthrough:
Two Types of Stickiness**
Water is polar, so hydrogen bonds form easily. Cohesion is water sticking to water. Adhesion is water sticking to something else, here the walls of the xylem vessels.

Holding the Column Together**
Xylem walls contain hydrophilic cellulose and lignin which attract water by adhesion. Together with cohesion between water molecules, this creates a continuous column that resists breaking under tension.

Moving Up as One**
When transpiration removes water from leaves, it exerts a pull (transpiration pull) on the column. Because of cohesion and adhesion, the whole column moves up together from roots to leaves without snapping.

Final answer: Hydrogen bonds cause cohesion between water molecules and adhesion of water to the hydrophilic cellulose / lignin walls of xylem vessels. This maintains an unbroken column of water that can be pulled up by transpiration pull.

Similar Pattern**
All three start at $0 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ at 06.00. All rise through the morning and fall in the late afternoon to evening. This mirrors the light intensity curve in Fig. 4.2B.

Clear Ranking**
At almost every time, emergent trees are highest, canopy trees intermediate, suppressed trees lowest. The difference is large. For example at 12.00 emergent is about $8.0 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ while canopy is about $3.2 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ and suppressed about $1.4 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$.

Quote Peaks With Units**
You must give numbers with units at least once. Emergent peaks at 14.30 at $8.5 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$. Canopy peaks at 14.30 at $3.5 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$. Suppressed peaks earlier at 13.00 at about $1.6-1.7 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$. Also note emergent shows the steepest increase, e.g. from about $4.9$ to $7.5 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ between 09.00 and 10.00.

Final answer: All trees have 0 transpiration rate at 06.00. All increase then decrease, peaking in early afternoon. Emergent peak $8.5 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ at 14.30, canopy peak $3.5 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ at 14.30, suppressed peak $1.6-1.7 \text{ kg h}^{-1}$ at 13.00. Emergent trees always have highest rate, suppressed lowest, with emergent much higher and showing steepest rise.

walkthrough:
Light and Stomata**
Emergent trees stick out above the canopy in Fig. 4.1 so receive full light intensity shown in Fig. 4.2B, while suppressed trees are shaded. Higher light causes stomata to open wider, allowing more water vapour loss. The reverse applies to suppressed trees.

Humidity, Temperature and Wind**
Above the canopy air is less humid, warmer and windier. Lower humidity means a steeper water potential gradient from leaf to air, so faster diffusion out. Higher temperature increases kinetic energy for evaporation and diffusion. Higher wind blows away the humid diffusion shell around leaves, keeping the gradient steep.

Size and Supply**
Emergent trees are larger with more leaves, so greater surface area and more stomata for loss. They also have longer / deeper roots to absorb and supply the extra water needed to sustain high transpiration. Suppressed trees have the opposite - sheltered, cool, humid microclimate plus smaller crowns.

Final answer: Emergent trees have higher rate because: higher light intensity gives wider stomatal aperture; lower humidity gives steeper water potential gradient; higher temperature gives faster evaporation / diffusion; higher wind speed removes humid air maintaining steep gradient. Also larger leaf area / more stomata and longer roots for water uptake.
